titulo: Buying: price, size, try it, change it
subtitulo: Four questions cover a shop — and the one about returns is the one you have to ask before you pay
cena: The shop is small, the owner is watching you decide, and you cannot tell whether picking it up yourself is normal here.
frasePiso: Ask the price, ask to try it, and ask about changing it — in that order, before the card comes out.

steps.pt: A shop is four questions long. How much, do you have my size, can I try it, and can I change it.

steps.acao: Greet back before saying what you want.

steps.pt: Dica pure means tell me what you need. Greet first — in a small shop, walking in silently reads as odd.

steps.promptPt: You want to browse without committing. Say so warmly. Speak now.
steps.pt: Good morning, I'm just having a look.

steps.promptPt: Nothing on this one has a tag. Use the frame from B11. Speak now.
It is close but tight. Ask about the next size up. Speak now.

steps.es: Solo la media e la large. Vuole provarla?
steps.pt: Only medium and large. Would you like to try it on?
steps.tts: Solo la media e la large. Vuole provarla?

steps.promptPt: Ask to try it on, using the frame from B06. Speak now.

steps.pt: Now the question people skip. Ask about changing it before you pay, not after — the answer differs by shop.

steps.promptPt: Ask whether you can exchange it if it does not fit. Speak now.
steps.es: Posso cambiarla se non va bene?
steps.pinyin: POS-so kam-bee-AR-la seh non va BEH-ne
steps.pt: Can I exchange it if it doesn't fit?
steps.tts: Posso cambiarla se non va bene?

steps.es: Entro otto giorni, con lo scontrino.
steps.pt: Within eight days, with the receipt.
steps.tts: Entro otto giorni, con lo scontrino.

steps.pt: With the receipt — again. In shops, at meals, in taxis, the scontrino is the thing that makes anything afterwards possible.

steps.promptPt: You like the shape, not the colour. Ask. Speak now.
Ask them to bring you a bag, using the frame from B14. Speak now.
steps.es: Mi porta una borsa, per favore?
steps.pinyin: mee POR-ta OO-na BOR-sa per fa-VO-re
steps.pt: Could you bring me a bag, please?
steps.tts: Mi porta una borsa, per favore?

steps.promptPt: You have decided not to buy. Leave without buying, warmly. Speak now.
steps.pt: I'll think about it, thank you very much.

steps.es: Quanto costa questa? Posso provarla? Posso cambiarla se non va bene?
steps.pinyin: KWAN-to KOS-ta KWES-ta. POS-so pro-VAR-la. POS-so kam-bee-AR-la seh non va BEH-ne
steps.pt: Shadow the three questions that finish a purchase.
steps.tts: Quanto costa questa? Posso provarla? Posso cambiarla se non va bene?

steps.pt: B15 done. Greet, ask the price, try it, ask about changing it — and ci penso lets you leave without buying.

secoes.corpo: In a small Italian shop the buongiorno is not optional politeness, it is how you register as a person rather than as traffic. Do solo un'occhiata then buys you the right to browse in peace.

exemplos.pt: Good morning, I'm just having a look.
I'll think about it, thanks very much.

secoes.corpo: Italian law guarantees a remedy for faulty goods, but a shop is not obliged to take back something you simply changed your mind about. Many will, within a window and with the receipt — which is exactly why you ask before you pay.

secoes.titulo: Ci penso is a complete exit
secoes.corpo: It means I'll think about it, and it is understood as a polite no without being one. Nobody expects an explanation for why you did not buy something.

The fourteen-day right of withdrawal that applies to online purchases in the EU does not extend to something you bought in person. In-store, the rule is whatever the shop told you, which is why you make them tell you.

permissao: You are allowed to walk out without buying. Ci penso, grazie is a complete and normal ending to a shop conversation in Italy — nobody is owed a purchase for the time they spent showing you two sizes.
espelho: Anyone who has bought something they did not want because leaving felt rude knows the pressure this part removes. It has nothing to do with Italian — it is the small-shop version of not wanting to disappoint someone who was nice to you.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You walk into a small shop and the owner greets you and stays near, rather than leaving you alone to browse.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I am being watched, or pressured to buy.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: In a small Italian shop the greeting and the attention are the service, and the customer is expected to greet back. Being left completely alone is closer to indifference than to respect.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say buongiorno and do solo un'occhiata. That answers the greeting and asks for room at the same time.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the space to look properly, and if you do want something you have already opened a conversation instead of starting cold.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in large chains or supermarkets, where staff genuinely do leave you alone and a greeting to the room would be unusual.
